related_questions.question: What is the standard treatment for IBD?
related_questions.snippet: Anti-inflammatory medicines Anti-inflammatories include aminosalicylates, such as mesalamine (Delzicol, Rowasa, others), balsalazide (Colazal) and olsalazine (Dipentum). Time-limited courses of corticosteroids also are used to induce remission. In addition to being anti-inflammatory, steroids are immunosuppressing.

related_questions.question: Which food is not good for IBD patients?
related_questions.snippet: Follow a low residue diet to relieve abdominal pain and diarrhea. If you have strictures, it is especially important to avoid nuts, seeds, beans and kernels. Avoid foods that may increase stool output such as fresh fruits and vegetables, prunes and caffeinated beverages. Cold foods may help reduce diarrhea.

related_questions.question: Does drinking a lot of water help with IBD?
related_questions.snippet: It is important to drink enough water to keep yourself well hydrated. Your IBD team may recommend that you add extra salt to your meals (around a teaspoon a day). Oral rehydration solutions (ORS) can be useful if you have short bowel syndrome or a high-output ileostomy.

text_blocks.snippet: The goal of IBD treatment is to reduce inflammation and induce or maintain remission, ultimately improving the patient's quality of life. Treatment typically involves medications and may include surgery. Various medications fall into categories like anti-inflammatories (including aminosalicylates and corticosteroids), immunomodulators, and biologics.
snippet_highlighted_words: Treatment typically involves medications and may include surgery

list.title: Anti-inflammatory medications:
list.snippet: Aminosalicylates (like mesalamine) are often a first-line treatment for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis. Corticosteroids (like prednisolone) are used to induce remission in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, but long-term use is not recommended due to potential side effects.

list.title: Immunomodulators:
list.snippet: These medications, such as azathioprine and methotrexate, help suppress the immune system's inflammatory response.

list.title: Biologics:
list.snippet: These are targeted therapies that block specific proteins involved in inflammation. Examples include anti-TNF agents (like infliximab, adalimumab, and golimumab), vedolizumab, ustekinumab, and others.

list.title: Biosimilars:
list.snippet: These are highly similar versions of existing biologics that can offer more affordable treatment options.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: While there's no one-size-fits-all diet, a well-balanced diet with a variety of nutrients is generally recommended. Some patients may benefit from a low-roughage diet or avoiding certain foods (like milk if lactose intolerant).

list.title: Surgery:
list.snippet: In some cases, surgery may be necessary to manage IBD, especially if medications are not effective or complications arise.

list.title: Individualized Approach:
list.snippet: The best treatment plan depends on the specific type of IBD (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis), the severity of the disease, and the patient's individual response to treatment.

list.title: Clinical Guidelines:
list.snippet: Guidelines from organizations like the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and Medscape provide evidence-based recommendations for managing IBD.

text_blocks.snippet: Example: For mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis, the AGA suggests using standard-dose mesalamine (oral and/or rectal). For moderate-to-severe cases, they recommend considering advanced therapies like biologics or immunomodulators.
